difficultyReason: Single-premise causal argument with one obvious gap: the lozenge's effect must explain the recoveries rather than the illness resolving on its own.
stimulus: Pediatrician: Every child in our clinic who received the new antiviral lozenge recovered from the sore throat within four days. So the lozenge must be effective at curing this type of sore throat.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the pediatrician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The children would not have recovered within four days without taking the lozenge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other antiviral treatment cures sore throats more quickly than the lozenge does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lozenge has been tested in clinics other than the pediatrician's.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sore throats of this type are caused by a virus rather than by bacteria.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every child who took the lozenge followed the dosing instructions exactly.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the lozenge for the recoveries. If the children would have recovered anyway in the same timeframe, the lozenge did nothing. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument claims the lozenge works, not that it is the fastest available treatment.
explanations.C: Out of scope — external replication is not a link in the pediatrician's reasoning.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — the argument is about whether the lozenge cures these sore throats, not about their underlying cause.
explanations.E: Defender disguised as strengthener — compliance would bolster the argument, but the pediatrician observed recoveries regardless of strict adherence.

difficultyReason: Single-premise ethical argument with one clear gap linking the premise's category (promise under duress) to the conclusion's category (contract under threat).
stimulus: Ethicist: A promise made under duress is not morally binding. Thus, the contract Mara signed while being threatened by her employer imposes no moral obligation on her.
questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mara's employer will face legal consequences for threatening her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contract signed under threatening conditions counts as a promise made under duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No contract is ever morally binding if one party benefits more than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mara intended to break the contract from the moment she signed it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contracts and promises differ in the legal obligations they create.

explanations.correct: The premise speaks of promises under duress; the conclusion is about a contract signed under threat. Without the bridge that such a contract qualifies as a promise made under duress, the premise does not reach the conclusion.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the argument is about moral obligation, not legal consequences for the employer.
explanations.C: Too strong — introduces a sweeping rule about benefit that the argument does not need.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Mara's intent is irrelevant to whether the contract binds her morally.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the ethicist's claim concerns moral, not legal, force.

difficultyReason: Straightforward economic analogy argument with one evident gap — conditions responsible for the cited town's outcome must carry over.
stimulus: Economist: When the neighboring town of Parrish raised its minimum wage last year, overall consumer spending in Parrish rose within six months. If our town raises its minimum wage by a similar amount, consumer spending here will also rise within six months.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parrish's minimum-wage increase was the largest in the region that year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer spending is the most important indicator of a town's economic health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No economic conditions unique to Parrish were responsible for the rise in spending there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every business in our town supports raising the minimum wage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our town has a larger population than Parrish does.

explanations.correct: The analogy needs the Parrish result to transfer. If something peculiar to Parrish caused the rise there, the inference to our town collapses. Negating C destroys the argument.
explanations.A: Out of scope — magnitude rank does not connect Parrish's outcome to ours.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not claim spending is the most important indicator, only that it will rise.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — business support is not a link in the economist's causal chain.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — if anything, the argument would prefer similarity of size, not a size difference.

difficultyReason: Single-premise legal argument with one obvious gap linking a statutory category to the specific case at issue.
stimulus: Attorney: The statute prohibits any commercial use of the public fountain. My client used the fountain as the backdrop for a paid photography shoot. Therefore, my client violated the statute.
questionStem: The attorney's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: using the fountain as a backdrop for a paid photography shoot is a commercial use of the fountain

choices.label: B
choices.text: the statute has been enforced against other photographers in the past

choices.label: C
choices.text: the client was aware of the statute at the time of the photo shoot

choices.label: D
choices.text: no public official granted the client permission to use the fountain

choices.label: E
choices.text: the fountain is the only public landmark covered by the statute

explanations.correct: The statute prohibits commercial use; the conclusion asserts a violation. Unless the photo shoot counts as commercial use, the premise cannot reach the conclusion. Negating A breaks the argument.
explanations.B: Out of scope — past enforcement patterns are not part of the reasoning.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument turns on what the client did, not on what the client knew.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — permission would rebut the charge, but the argument does not need to rule it out to connect its premise to its conclusion.
explanations.E: Out of scope — coverage of other landmarks is irrelevant to whether this use violated the statute.

difficultyReason: Single-premise causal inference with one obvious chronological alternative that must be ruled out.
stimulus: Ecologist: Populations of the spotted salamander have declined sharply in ponds where a certain pesticide has been detected. So the pesticide must be responsible for the decline of the spotted salamander in those ponds.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ecologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pesticide was present in these ponds before the salamander populations began to decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pesticide is more harmful to salamanders than to any other amphibian.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salamander populations have not declined in any pond where the pesticide is absent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pesticide will eventually cause the salamander to become extinct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulators intend to ban the pesticide in response to the ecologist's findings.

explanations.correct: For the pesticide to be responsible, it must have been present before the decline, not after. Negate A — the pesticide arrived after the decline — and it cannot be the cause.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only claims the pesticide is responsible in these ponds, not that it is uniquely harmful.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument does not need declines to happen exclusively in pesticide ponds; other causes elsewhere are allowed.
explanations.D: Out of scope — extinction projections are not part of the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — regulatory response is unrelated to whether the pesticide caused the observed decline.

difficultyReason: Single-premise inference from a test result to a product property, with one evident gap about what the test actually measures.
stimulus: Reviewer: The new laptop ran every benchmark program we tried without slowing down once. So this laptop is powerful enough for any task our readers are likely to perform.
questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The benchmark programs collectively demand at least as much of the laptop as any task the readers are likely to perform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The laptop is priced within the range most readers can afford.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other laptop on the market outperformed this one on the benchmarks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Benchmark programs have improved significantly over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most readers have previously owned a laptop from the same manufacturer.

explanations.correct: The conclusion extrapolates from benchmarks to real-world tasks. Without the assumption that the benchmarks are at least as demanding as those tasks, the benchmark success tells us nothing about readers' tasks.
explanations.B: Out of scope — price is not linked to the laptop's power.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about sufficiency for readers' tasks, not about ranking among competitors.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — trend data on benchmarks is not used by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — prior ownership has no bearing on the laptop's capability.

difficultyReason: Single-premise dating inference with one obvious gap: the inscription and the tablet must be contemporaneous.
stimulus: Linguist: The inscription on this stone tablet is written in Old Phrygian, and every known Old Phrygian inscription dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE. Therefore, this tablet dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No language other than Old Phrygian used a writing system that resembled the one on the tablet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inscription was not added to the tablet long after the tablet itself was made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most Old Phrygian inscriptions are found on stone rather than on other materials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tablet was discovered in a region where Old Phrygian was spoken.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Old Phrygian is closely related to the language now called Modern Phrygian.

explanations.correct: The inscription's date only dates the tablet if the two were made at the same time. Negate B — the inscription was added much later — and the tablet itself could be far older or younger than the inscription.
explanations.A: Defender disguised as strengthener — misidentification would undermine the argument, but the stimulus already stipulates the inscription is in Old Phrygian.
explanations.C: Out of scope — typical material of Old Phrygian inscriptions is irrelevant to this tablet's date.
explanations.D: Out of scope — where the tablet was found is not a link in the dating inference.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — a relationship to a modern language has no bearing on the dating of Old Phrygian inscriptions.

difficultyReason: Single-premise historical inference with one obvious gap about what the document actually reports.
stimulus: Historian: A letter written by General Halpern on June 3, 1794, describes his troops marching through the town of Valcour that morning. Therefore, Halpern's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Halpern's letter accurately describes where his troops were on the day it was written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halpern personally marched alongside his troops as they passed through Valcour.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other general's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Halpern wrote letters describing his troops' movements on most days of the campaign.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The town of Valcour was strategically important to both sides in the conflict.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the letter as a reliable report. If the letter misstates where the troops were that morning, the conclusion does not follow. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Halpern's personal location is not what the conclusion claims.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the argument does not require Halpern's troops to be the only ones present.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the historian needs one accurate letter, not a pattern of letter-writing.
explanations.E: Out of scope — strategic importance has nothing to do with where the troops actually were.

difficultyReason: Single-premise policy argument with one clear gap between program goal and program adoption.
stimulus: City planner: Residents have said repeatedly that their top priority is reducing traffic congestion downtown. The proposed congestion-pricing plan would reduce traffic congestion downtown. Therefore, the city should adopt the congestion-pricing plan.
questionStem: The city planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should adopt any plan that advances residents' top priority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing has successfully reduced traffic in every city that has tried it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents would be willing to pay significantly higher fees to drive downtown.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plan would reduce congestion more effectively than any alternative the city is considering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The planner was hired specifically to address downtown traffic congestion.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from a plan that advances residents' top priority to the conclusion that the city should adopt it. Without a principle connecting those two, the premises do not support the conclusion. Negating A blocks the inference.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not require universal success, only that this plan will reduce congestion.
explanations.C: Out of scope — willingness to pay is not invoked in the reasoning.
explanations.D: Too strong — the planner claims the plan should be adopted, not that it is the best available option.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the planner's hiring is not a link in the argument.

difficultyReason: Single-premise attribution argument with one obvious gap linking stylistic features to authorship.
stimulus: Art historian: The brushwork on this newly examined landscape displays all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings. So this landscape was painted by Vermeer.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No painter other than Vermeer produces brushwork displaying all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vermeer painted more landscapes than any other subject during his career.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The landscape was found in a location where Vermeer is known to have worked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The canvas and pigments used in the landscape are consistent with those available in Vermeer's lifetime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Art historians can identify any painting's creator on the basis of brushwork alone.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Vermeer's authorship from brushwork features. If another painter could produce the same distinctive features, the inference fails. Negating A destroys the argument.
explanations.B: Out of scope — the frequency of Vermeer's landscapes does not help link this painting's brushwork to him.
explanations.C: Defender disguised as strengthener — location would bolster attribution, but the stylistic argument does not depend on it.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — material consistency would support the attribution, but it is not what the brushwork inference turns on.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument claims this painting is a Vermeer, not that brushwork alone identifies every painting.
